title: When Is Program Structure Required? Certificate-Grounded Calibration of Program-Induction Difficulty
comment: 26 pages, 1 figure, 24 tables, including appendices. Code and reproduction artifacts at https://github.com/dqswordman/program-structure-certificates
summary: A program-induction benchmark is informative when its examples require the structure it aims to test. Yet a two-rule generator can produce demonstrations that a single rule also explains. We introduce certificate-grounded calibration, which constructs matched tasks with minimum solution lengths of one and two in a bounded string-replacement language. Complete one-rule enumeration and an executable two-rule witness certify the change before model inference. We evaluate 120 reference families with three to six shared examples, using 1,440 new model trajectories and 480 saved trajectories. Across Qwen3-8B and Olmo-3-7B-Think, displayed-task completion is 23.53-45.83 percentage points lower on certified separation tasks, while success on a wholly unshown witness pair is 8.40-13.45 points higher. These witness gains accompany lower agreement on uniformly sampled strings and 1.93-5.78% agreement on inputs that activate both reference rules. Recertification also reveals that a single unchanged example can exclude a shortcut and determine whether two rules are required. Together, these results show how the evidence supplied by examples shapes both the required solution and the programs models produce. The construction provides an executable testbed for comparing program search, final-answer delivery, and behavior on new inputs under verified task requirements.

title: Mode Inference for Substructural Adjoint Types
summary:
Adjoint types [Jang et al. 2024] provide a method of mixing substructural modes (for example, linear, affine, strict, or unrestricted) in a type system while preserving the proof-theoretic and computational properties of each mode. Uses of such a system include performing compiler optimizations or providing safety guarantees on parts of a program whose modes support them, while not restricting the programmer's ability to write other code as they usually do. However, Jang et al.'s algorithmic type system is monomorphic in the modes, requiring the programmer to anticipate a potentially large number of combinations of modes, and possibly copy code to conform to each of them.
  In this paper we define a mode inference algorithm for programs with adjoint types that produces principal modes, summarizing all possible substructural modes of a function in a simple constraint language. This removes the burden from the programmer to a priori analyze the substructural properties of their code, and, furthermore, allows a single function definition to subsume all its instances at different modes. We show that our system is sound and complete with respect to a mild restriction of Jang et al.'s monomorphic version.

title: Tenon: A Unified Programming Framework for Retargetable PIM Compilation
summary: Processing-in-memory (PIM) is emerging as a building block of heterogeneous systems for memory-bound workloads, and commercial prototypes now span near-bank SIMD engines, bank-level GDDR accelerators, programmable DRAM cores, and bit-level in-SRAM processors. Their programming stacks are fragmented: no abstraction or compiler is shared across vendors, and per-device models range from instruction sequences to C-like languages. Data layout further complicates the problem: tight compute-memory integration makes data layout a first-order optimization, yet existing PIM compilers lack a unified way to represent and optimize it. A key observation is that PIM compilation targets can be modeled as nested grids of compute and storage units connected by legal data-transfer paths. We present Tenon, a unified programming framework for retargetable PIM compilation. It decouples workload, compilation target, and cost specifications, so a workload is expressed once and compiled through a unified programming framework. Tenon generalizes the $\mathbb{F}_2$ linear layout algebra from GPU compilers to map logical work and data onto these compute and storage grids. It automatically constructs a minimum-movement data layout given a workload and a target specification. We evaluate Tenon on six PIM backends: five commercial backends and AttAcc, a state-of-the-art academic HBM-based PIM architecture. Across the commercial backends, it matches or outperforms vendor, expert, and compiler baselines, with geometric-mean speedups of up to $1.20\times$ and individual speedups up to $3.65\times$. For end-to-end GPT-13B decoding on AttAcc, Tenon-compiled workloads run $1.2$--$1.3\%$ faster than those compiled by DCC, a state-of-the-art PIM compiler, across all three batch-4 configurations. Together, these results demonstrate Tenon's performance portability across diverse PIM target families.

title: Sightline: Calibrated Data-Flow Summaries for LLM-Integrated Applications
summary: Programs increasingly call large language models (LLMs), filling prompt placeholders with program values and consuming the output. Such a call crosses the boundary between natural language and programming language (NL/PL). To follow data across it, an analysis needs a data-flow summary of which placeholders the output uses, but no code describes what the model does. Analyses of these LLM-integrated applications therefore taint every output with every input, creating spurious flows, or ask a second model to label each call, which is costly. We prove, and mechanize in Lean 4, that a placeholder flows to the output of a transformer, to first order, only through the attention that reads it (no reading, no flow), and that a faint reading or sensitivity cannot certify that a placeholder does not flow. Unlike reading, the log-probability gradients and Fisher signals of existing methods vanish on confident outputs, and single-span removal fails on duplicated content. Our tool, Sightline, reads a recorded call in one forward pass, learns from labels which reads are uses, and calibrates the pruning to miss at most a chosen fraction $α$ of true flows, on average over call sites, when deployment is exchangeable with calibration. On 2,103 unseen repository families and four models, Sightline is the most accurate summary against the seven closest methods and a hidden-state probe. Calibrated at $α$ = 1%, it misses about 1% of true flows and prunes 43.9-65.6% of spurious flows, 1.6 to 2.6 times as many as the best baseline, and still 43.8-60.1% when calibrated on another collection. Through an open surrogate, it reads models treated as closed about as accurately as they read themselves, without their labels. In the information-flow control of an LLM agent, it removes about half of the labels from inputs that do not flow.

title: You Have Mail: Set-Theoretic Types for Actors
summary:
We present a type system for the processes of Elixir, a dynamic language based on the actor model whose static type system covers only its functional core. Each process is typed by $\mathtt{pid}(t)$, where the ``interface'' $t$ is the type of the messages the process expects in its mailbox: sends are checked against the recipient's interface, and receives rely on the interface of the process that performs them.
  One of the difficulties of typing Elixir is that mailboxes are implicit: a function shipped in a message may evaluate $\mathtt{self()}$ and execute receive instructions, and both refer to whichever process eventually runs the function---$\mathtt{self()}$ returns that process's pid, receive reads that process's mailbox---so the mailbox they act on is not known where the function is written. We solve this problem by inferring, for every function, bounds on the type of the mailboxes it can be used with; as a result, the system types higher-order functions that travel in messages even when they contain reference to $\mathtt{self()}$ and receive instructions.
  The only new annotation the programmer writes is the interface of each spawned process; everything else is inferred by reusing the existing subtyping and constraint-resolution machinery of Elixir, and the system is proved sound.
  For legacy code, the interface can be reconstructed from the receive clauses: what the branches do with their messages bounds it from above, and the most permissive solution is sharp enough to recover received pids and closures.
